clue.text: 'ow, so to speak, to line threadbare carriage?

indicators.note: the exclamation is set inside the worn-out word, lining it like cloth inside a coat

parts.note: threadbare means bare, worn down to nothing
'ow is a dropped-aitch way of saying 'how', but read as a cry of pain it is ouch

explanation.surface: A Cockney asks how one might line a worn-out old carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to line' is the container signal: the exclamation sits within the worn-out word, splitting it near its end.
explanation.definitionFit: A barouche is a four-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle with a folding hood, a kind of carriage.

clue.text: Sexy woman has it off in the bank

indicators.note: the words it and off are placed inside the word for a bank

parts.note: a bluff is a steep bank or cliff
taken as written

explanation.surface: A suggestive tale of a woman making love on a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has it off' looks like slang for sex, but 'has' is only a link and the rest goes in the bank.
explanation.definitionFit: Bit of fluff is dated British slang for an attractive young woman.

clue.text: Go a long way in on drug and pay this to come back out?

definitions.text: pay this to come back out?

indicators.note: the pieces for go and a long way are placed within those for on and drug

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a letter heading
E is short for ecstasy, a drug
a go is a turn, as in a game
far means a long way

explanation.surface: Someone travels far after taking drugs and wonders what it costs to get home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the go-plus-distance pair between the two short pieces; the question mark flags the loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The fare for a journey home is what you pay to come back from a trip out.

clue.text: Consume on or before this Tuesday — be alert!

indicators.note: alert suggests something lively and stirred up, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A notice warns that something must be eaten by Tuesday, so stay watchful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alert' rearranges TUESDAY and BE.
explanation.definitionFit: Food labels print a use-by date, the last day the contents should be eaten.

clue.text: After interminable period, prepare to be introduced to what Singer does in party

indicators.note: the remaining pieces follow the shortened time word
without an end, so the last letter of the time word is dropped

parts.note: an hour is a period of time

indicators.note: the word for prepare is put inside the word for what Singer does

parts.note: Singer is a well-known make of sewing machine, so it does sewing
to arm is to prepare for battle

explanation.surface: After a long wait, a guest gets ready to join a party where a singer performs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interminable' docks the last letter of the period, and 'to be introduced to' sets prepare inside the stitching. 'Singer' looks like a vocalist but is the sewing-machine brand.
explanation.definitionFit: A housewarming is a party held to celebrate moving into a new home.

clue.text: See 15
For living I circulate and ring round Pan-American district

indicators.note: the word for ring goes around the two other pieces

parts.note: to ring is to bell, as in giving someone a bell
a pan is a toilet bowl, so a loo
DC, the District of Columbia, is the American capital district

explanation.surface: An odd claim about circulating and phoning around a Pan-American area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pan-American' reads as one word, but splits into a toilet pan and the US capital's district, both rung round.
explanation.definitionFit: Blood cells are carried around the body by circulation and are essential to life.

clue.text: See 24
See 22
Did quick sum, as Steptoes did on the way to London

parts.note: Steptoe and Son was a British sitcom about rag-and-bone men, who went totting, collecting saleable junk
travelling up is going towards London, the capital

explanation.surface: Someone does a quick calculation, like rag-and-bone men heading for the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Steptoe and Son was a British TV comedy about scrap dealers; 'totting' is their trade of collecting refuse to sell.
explanation.definitionFit: To tot up is to add figures together, a quick bit of arithmetic.

clue.text: Tree-dweller procuring a copper utensil

indicators.note: the tree animal takes in the letter, gaining it inside

parts.note: a potto is a small tree-dwelling African primate
peeler is old British slang for a policeman, after Robert Peel

explanation.surface: A tree animal obtains a copper kitchen tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'procuring' has the primate take in the letter; 'copper' looks like the metal but is a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A potato peeler is a kitchen tool for removing skin from vegetables.

clue.text: This could put team-mate in trouble — and it has! Op modified records, when admitted

definitions.text: This could put team-mate in trouble

indicators.note: changed in form, so these letters are rearranged
the word for when is let inside the word for records

parts.note: LPs are long-playing records
as can mean when, as in 'as I arrived'

explanation.surface: A hospital patient's notes are altered after an operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'modified' rearranges IT HAS OP; 'admitted' lets when into records. The surface hints at medical records.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby or football, a hospital pass reaches a team-mate just as an opponent is about to tackle them hard.

clue.text: Street in Theatreland holding clue to "The Meaning of Life"?

definitions.text: Street in Theatreland holding clue to "The Meaning of Life"?

parts.words: Street in Theatreland holding clue to "The Meaning of Life"?
parts.note: a numbered Broadway street, whose number is the answer to life in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy

explanation.surface: A New York theatre street seems to hold the secret of existence.
explanation.walkthrough: In Douglas Adams's Hitchhiker's Guide, the computer's answer to life, the universe and everything is the number 42.
explanation.definitionFit: Manhattan's theatre district includes the famous street numbered 42, the subject of a musical.

clue.text: Risk writer's taken up in drink — perishes, disfigured at the end

indicators.note: the turned writer is placed inside the word for drink

parts.note: a jar is British slang for a drink

indicators.note: in a down clue taken up means read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the American writer

indicators.note: the tail of the word is spoiled, its final letter shifted out of place

parts.note: dies means perishes

explanation.surface: A writer is tipsy, and his death is a messy ending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken up' reverses the writer, as a down clue reads upwards; 'disfigured at the end' shifts the final S of perishes one place.
explanation.definitionFit: To jeopardise something is to put it at risk.

clue.text: Cover for schoolboy having swallowed 10, they say

indicators.note: signals that the word for having swallowed is heard, not spelt

parts.note: eaten means having swallowed
10 across is a potato, and a jacket is a baked potato in its skin

explanation.surface: A schoolboy's coat has somehow consumed a potato, people claim.
explanation.walkthrough: An Eton jacket is the short jacket once worn by younger boys at Eton, the English public school; 'they say' makes EATEN sound like ETON.
explanation.definitionFit: The short black jacket worn by junior boys at Eton College is a garment covering a schoolboy.

clue.text: Deceitfulness involving female's somewhat cold and hard to take — and then you die

indicators.note: the word for deceitfulness wraps around the letter for female

parts.note: lies are acts of deceit
F is the abbreviation for female
a bit means somewhat
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A cynic describes deceit, coldness and hardship ending in death.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition completes the saying: the full phrase ends 'and then you die'.
explanation.definitionFit: The cynical saying runs in full 'Life's a bitch and then you die', so the closing words point to its first half.

clue.text: Completely clear pub to accommodate band? The opposite

indicators.note: one word takes another inside it
reverses the roles, so the band holds the pub rather than the pub holding the band

parts.note: a stripe is a band of colour
a bar is a pub

explanation.surface: A landlord empties the pub to fit in a band, or rather the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, BAR should hold the band; 'The opposite' swaps it, so STRIPE holds BAR.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip bare is to remove everything, leaving a place completely cleared.

clue.text: Now attending repeatedly

parts.note: to be at an event is to attend it
present means in attendance

explanation.surface: Someone is now attending over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repeatedly' tells you to use 'attending' twice, once as AT and once as PRESENT.
explanation.definitionFit: At present is an idiom meaning now, at this moment.

clue.text: Would Afrit's anagram have disentangled this? Absolutely not!

parts.words: Would Afrit's anagram have disentangled this?
parts.note: the letters of Afrit, the famous setter, are a jumble of a short word and it, and that jumble set apart from it reads as the phrase

explanation.surface: Asks whether the old setter Afrit could have solved this.
explanation.walkthrough: Afrit was the pen name of A.F. Ritchie, a celebrated Listener setter; his name rearranged gives the first and last words, with FROM between.
explanation.definitionFit: Far from it is an emphatic idiom of denial, like no way.

clue.text: Reporter's goin' around a plant

indicators.note: a reporter's words are spoken, so what follows is heard

parts.note: loopin', with a dropped g, means going around

explanation.surface: A journalist goes round a plant, speaking casually.
explanation.definitionFit: The lupin is a garden flower with tall spikes of blooms.

clue.text: Congestion Zone? Infringements here may lead to on-the-spot punishment

definitions.meaning: a crowded box in front of goal, packed with players at set pieces

definitions.text: Infringements here may lead to on-the-spot punishment
definitions.meaning: a foul by defenders in this box gives a kick from the penalty spot

explanation.surface: Breaking traffic rules in London's charging zone brings instant fines.
explanation.walkthrough: The Congestion Zone is central London's charging area for cars; here it is the crowded box in football.
explanation.definitionFit: The football box in front of goal is a crowded zone where fouls lead to spot kicks.

clue.text: Poet put one "t" in "affirmative"

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the word for affirmative

parts.note: yes is an affirmative answer
a means one
the letter T as written

explanation.surface: Instructions to insert a single letter into a word meaning yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put one t' gives A T, which goes inside YES.
explanation.definitionFit: W.B. Yeats was an Irish poet and Nobel laureate.

clue.text: Double joint provided by this cook, trimming edge (hot)

indicators.note: the cook surrounds the other pieces like a trimming around their edges

parts.note: taken as written
a lip is an edge, as of a jug
H is the abbreviation for hot on taps

explanation.surface: A cook trims the edge of a joint of meat while it is hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trimming' has the cook surround edge and hot just after his first letter. 'joint' suggests meat but means a connection.
explanation.definitionFit: A clip hook is a pair of hooks that close together, giving a double fastening.

clue.text: See 3
Misconduct, when filling metal carrier?

indicators.note: the word for when is put in between the metal and the carrier

parts.note: lead is a metal
a tray carries things
as can mean when

explanation.surface: Bad behaviour while something is poured into a metal container.
explanation.walkthrough: 'filling' sets when between metal and carrier. 'Misconduct' reads as a noun but is a verb: to conduct wrongly.
explanation.definitionFit: To lead astray is to guide someone wrongly, to misconduct them as a verb.

clue.text: I have pink and white flowers for St David's Day, which cuts the work in two

definitions.text: I have pink and white flowers

indicators.note: the date breaks into the word for work
the word for work is split into two parts by the date

parts.note: a task is a piece of work
St David's Day, Wales's national day, is March 1st, written MAR I

explanation.surface: A plant boasts of flowering on Wales's national day, interrupting the work.
explanation.walkthrough: St David's Day, Wales's national day, falls on 1 March, written as a month and Roman numeral; 'cuts' and 'in two' split the work around it.
explanation.definitionFit: The tamarisk is a shrub bearing feathery sprays of small pink or white flowers.

clue.text: See 10
The writer's opinion is that this is not unimportant to fantasise either

indicators.note: something not unimportant to the words is integral to them, so the answer lies inside

explanation.surface: A writer gives a view about fantasising and its importance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is not unimportant to' means integral to, so the answer is within 'fantasise either'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase introduces the speaker's own view, so it means in my opinion.
